item.content:encoded: The market reaction to the Tata Steel–APL Apollo Tubes deal was very negative with shares of both companies seeing selloffs. This is a complex deal. APL Apollo will first buy Tata Steel’s tubes & colour business (TSCL) for ₹28,000 crore. Then Tata Steel will buy APL Apollo for about ₹32,267 crore in a transaction that includes buying out the latter’s promoters and an open offer. It implies about ₹4,200 crore in new liabilities for Tata Steel.

item.title: Sanofi's $41 bn Insmed deal aims to secure growth beyond Dupixent
item.description: Sanofi's $41 billion acquisition of Insmed will expand its respiratory drug portfolio as the French drugmaker seeks growth beyond blockbuster Dupixent.
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Sanofi's $41 bn Insmed deal aims to secure growth beyond Dupixent

Sanofi's $41 bn Insmed deal aims to secure growth beyond Dupixent Sanofi's $41 billion acquisition of Insmed will expand its respiratory drug portfolio as the French drugmaker seeks growth beyond blockbuster Dupixent.

Sanofi's $41 billion acquisition of Insmed marks its biggest deal in two decades, strengthening its respiratory drug portfolio as CEO Belen Garijo seeks to reduce the company's reliance on blockbuster Dupixent. (Photo:Reuters)

Reuters 4 min read Last Updated : Nov 24 2026 | 11:15 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Sanofi will buy US drugmaker Insmed for $41 billion in cash, it said on Tuesday, its biggest deal in two decades as CEO Belen Garijo seeks to turn around the French firm and find new sources of growth beyond blockbuster drug Dupixent. The deal, at a 17.5% premium to Insmed's last closing price, marks a bold bet by Garijo, Sanofi's first female CEO, who took the helm in May with a mandate to fix the company's drug pipeline and arrest a share price slide. Insmed focuses on respiratory drugs. "Finally Sanofi is doing the deal everyone expected," said Claus Henrik Johansen, CEO of Global Health Invest, a Danish healthcare investment fund which holds Sanofi shares.

"Investors have a glimpse at the 'after-Dupixent' Sanofi," he said, as Sanofi's shares jumped by around 6% on Tuesday. Also Read

Nexus Select Trust acquires Kolkata's Diamond Plaza Mall for ₹355 crore

CrowdStrike to acquire Zscaler in record $43.9 billion all-stock deal

FSSAI suspends licences of five nutraceutical firms over safety violations

Clinical trials beyond metros: Balancing growth, ethics and patient safety premium

Revamped medical device PLI to boost localisation, widen manufacturing base

Still, Johansen said more clinical data and sales projections were needed to support the valuation. Eczema drug Dupixent generated sales of over €15 billion ($16.4 billion) last year, almost 40% of Sanofi's total. Since taking over, Garijo has launched a strategic review, overhauled the executive committee and expanded a deal with long-time partner Regeneron to settle prior litigation, seen as another win for the CEO. Sanofi's shares lost ground in Garijo's first few months, but have shot up 20% since the start of October and are now up 12% since she started.

"We are executing with discipline and with vigour," Garijo said.   SANOFI'S BIGGEST DEAL IN 20 YEARS Sanofi's $175 per share deal for Insmed is 46% above the price on November 18, the day before Bloomberg News first reported Sanofi was weighing a possible acquisition. The French drugmaker will fund the acquisition through a combination of debt and cash on hand, and has secured committed financing in support of the transaction. "The deal is the fourth-largest deal in cash in Europe ever, and the first largest in cash in France," Sanofi finance chief François Roger told journalists. JPMorgan was the exclusive financial advisor to Sanofi on the deal, it said.

The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027 and to be accretive to earnings per share by the end of 2028, Sanofi said. It estimates annual cost benefits of more than $500 million from the deal, Roger said. "Insmed is an excellent strategic fit for Sanofi," said Markus Manns, portfolio manager at Sanofi investor Union Investment, adding the deal would help Garijo deal with the Dupixent patent cliff and the weak pipeline. "Acquiring Insmed would address both objectives." The deal also follows the appointment of Sanofi's former chief executive, Paul Hudson, to Insmed's board in October. 'IT BUYS TIME' Analysts welcomed the deal, saying Sanofi could fund it without putting its dividend or credit rating at risk.

Sanofi shares were up 6% at €90 by 0915 GMT, the top gainer on Europe's benchmark STOXX 600 index. Berenberg analyst Luisa Hector said the transaction was a great fit for Sanofi, citing Insmed's respiratory focus, early commercial assets and pipeline. Brokerage Jefferies was more circumspect and said it was not a silver bullet. "The deal does not fix Sanofi's R&D/pipeline questions, but it buys time," it wrote. After the acquisition, the combined group expects to generate enough cash to pay down its debt quickly and retain flexibility to invest in early-stage acquisitions. RESPIRATORY DRUG PIPELINE Insmed has two approved respiratory medicines on the market. Brinsupri treats non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis, while Arikayce treats refractory mycobacterium avium complex lung disease.

Garijo said the portfolio offered combined peak sales potential that was expected to exceed $10 billion through the end of the next decade. "We have a global commercial reach, experience in respiratory diseases, and patient support capabilities to help ensure marketed medicines reach even more patients and realise their full potential," she added. CFO Roger said Sanofi planned to retain flexibility for bolt-on acquisitions to complement its existing pipeline, particularly for early-stage assets in immunology, rare diseases and vaccines.

item.content:encoded:
Home / Economy / News / India, China set for record Russian oil imports in 2026 amid Iran war

India, China set for record Russian oil imports in 2026 amid Iran war Seaborne Russian oil shipments to the two countries averaged 3.4 million barrels per day through mid-November, up 530,000 bpd from a year earlier, but are expected to ease in 2027

Russia's oil exports are expected to rise 6 per cent in 2026 to 244.7 million metric tons

Reuters 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 24 2026 | 3:13 PM IST

Listen to This Article

India and China are on track for record Russian oil imports this year, plugging a supply gap caused by the Iran war, as US sanctions waivers eased purchases and Ukrainian drone attacks knocked out Russian refining, according to tanker data and industry sources. But traders and analysts expect shipments to Russia's two biggest customers to wane in 2027 as Middle Eastern supplies recover and reclaim market share. Seaborne Russian oil supplies to the world's two most populous countries averaged 3.4 million barrels per day this year through mid-November, up about 530,000 bpd from a year earlier, according to Vortexa Analytics. With Brent crude up nearly one third since the start of the war, the increased volumes, which include Kazakhstan oil transited via Russian ports, have bolstered Moscow's oil revenue even as repeated drone attacks by Kiev have hit nearly half of Russian refining capacity, prompting more crude exports.

Russia's oil exports are expected to rise 6 per cent in 2026 to 244.7 million metric tons, or about 4.9 million bpd, according to a forecast by its Ministry of Economic Development. Also Read

Oil, gas import bill up 60% in Oct as Brent surges, LPG use declines

Ukraine's window shortage leaves war-damaged homes exposed to winter cold

Russian missiles, drones land in Poland, Nato calls it a 'violation'

Russian strikes on Kyiv kill three, injure nine and disrupt power supply

Russia open to Nato-like security guarantees for Ukraine: US envoy

Temporary US waivers on Russian oil sanctions, aimed at keeping markets supplied amid the Middle East crisis, widened the pool of vessels and suppliers available to India and China, allowing them to increase purchases. Together, the two bought more than 80 per cent of Russia's crude exports, according to estimates by two industry sources familiar with Russian oil flows. Russia supplies a quarter of China's imports Russian oil exports to top overall buyer China rose 17 per cent to 2.34 million bpd during January-October, worth $59.6 billion, accounting for about a quarter of Beijing's oil imports, according to Chinese customs data, despite a 15 per cent fall in its crude imports as Middle Eastern supplies plunged.

"Lower shipping risks and greater supply reliability have been the main reasons behind the increase in China's Russian crude imports since the war broke out," said Muyu Xu, analyst with tanker tracker Kpler. However, Michal Meidan, head of China Energy Research at the Oxford Institute of Energy Studies, predicted China's appetite will wane in 2027 as Russia's surging import share exceeds Beijing's comfort zone with a single supplier. "More importantly, they are no longer at a discount and are trading at higher premiums to Brent than Gulf crudes. The teapots can no longer afford them," said Meidan, referring to smaller independent Chinese refiners that rely on discounted crude.

"As Gulf flows stabilise, Chinese refiners will revert back to those crudes and are already favouring Brazilian grades," she added. Strong demand for Russian barrels, spurred also by dwindling Iranian oil flows due to the US naval blockade, lifted spot premiums of ESPO to as high as nearly $30 a barrel over ICE Brent for deliveries into east China. India's record Russian purchases India, the top buyer of seaborne Russian crude, averaged imports of 1.99 million bpd through early November, up 250,000 bpd annually, Kpler data showed, despite cutting purchases earlier this year after a threatened hike in US tariffs. During January to October, India's Russian oil imports rose about 10 per cent to 1.87 million bpd, about 38 per cent of overall volumes, according to data from trade sources.

India's Russian oil imports are likely to average 1.9 million bpd in 2026, sources at Indian refiners said. India's purchases are likely to return to pre-Iran war levels in 2027 if supplies from the Middle East normalise, with imports expected to be driven by prices, the sources said.
